chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, altogether from Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Ayoub al-Khazzaz, from Yazeed al-Kunasy, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who pronounced Zihar from his wife, then divorced her with a single divorce. He (peace be upon him) said: 'When he divorces her with a single divorce, the Zihar becomes invalid, and the divorce demolishes the Zihar.'

He (the narrator) said, 'So I said, 'Is there for him to revert to her?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Yes, she is his wife. So if he were to revert back to her, it would obligate upon him what obligates upon the perpetrator of Zihar from before they touch each other.' I said, 'So if he were to leave her until her term expires and she is in control of herself, then he maries her after that, would the Zihar necessitate upon him before he touches her?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'No. She was irrevocably divorced from him, and in control of herself.'

I said, 'So if he does Zihar from her, and does not touch her, and leaves her, not touching her except that he sees her naked without touching her, would anything from that necessitate upon him?' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'She is his wife, and it is not prohibited on him copulating with her, but it obligates upon him what obligates upon the perpetrator of Zihar, before he copulates with her, and she is his wife.'

I said, 'Supposing if she were to raise it to the Sultan (ruler) and says, 'This is my husband, and he had done Zihar from me, and has kept me, not touching me fearing that it would obligate upon him what obligates upon the perpetrator of Zihar'.' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'It is not upon him that he should be compelled to emancipation, and fasting, and feeding, if there does not happen to be for him what he can emancipate with, and give charity with, from before he touches her, and from after having touched her.'
He (peace be upon him) said: 'So if he is able to emancipate, then it is upon the Imam to compel him to emancipation and charity, from before he touches her, and from after he touches her.'

key_terms.السُّلْطَان: As-sultan: The ruler or judge, who can compel the husband to perform the expiation.
key_terms.الصِّيَام: As-siyam: Fasting, another form of expiation for Zihar.
key_terms.الْإِطْعَام: Al-it'am: Feeding the poor, the third form of expiation for Zihar.
key_terms.تَطْلِيقَة: Tatliqah: A single, revocable divorce pronouncement.
key_terms.ظِهَار: Zihar: A pre-Islamic and early Islamic form of divorce where a husband likens his wife's back to his mother's back, prohibiting sexual intercourse until expiation is made.
key_terms.عِتْق: Itq: Emancipation of a slave, one of the forms of expiation for Zihar.

ai.seo_question: What is the effect of a single divorce on the validity of Zihar and the subsequent expiation obligations?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the interplay between Zihar and Talaq, establishing that a single revocable divorce nullifies the Zihar bond while preserving the marital status, thereby requiring the expiation before consummation upon reconciliation. It further distinguishes the ruling for irrevocable divorce where the wife gains full autonomy, and clarifies that mere visual intimacy without physical contact still obligates the expiation, reflecting the Shia juristic emphasis on the husband's capacity to fulfill the kaffarah under the Imam's supervision.
